# Box Sizing

#### Course: Learn CSS

## Box Sizing

By default, padding and borders are not included in an element's width and height.

This means if you set a width of 300px and add padding or borders, the actual size will be larger than 300px.

![Box Sizing Calculation](data:image/png;base64,)

##### How does it work?

Ambika Pravin Sonawane

##### How the actual size will be larger than 300px ? Can you please explain me the calculation of the box sizing.

![User profile picture](data:image/png;base64,)

Udayan Shakya from Programiz

Hi Ambika! Yes, box-sizing can be a bit confusing at the very beginning.

When you set an element's width to 300px, that value only accounts for the content area by default. However, the full size of the element is determined by adding the padding, border, and margin to this width.

Here's how you can calculate the actual width of a box:

```css
content_width
+ padding_left
+ padding_right
+ border_left
+ border_right
= actual_width
```

The same formula applies to height.

Let's break it down with the example given in the image in the course:

- You have a width of 300px.
- Then, you have a padding of 50px on each side.
- Finally, there's a border of 50px on each side.

Then, the total width calculation would be:

```css
300px (content)
+ 50px (left padding)
+ 50px (right padding)
+ 50px (left border)
+ 50px (right border)
= 500px
```

This makes the actual box appear larger than 300px when displayed since the total width is actually 500px.

Note: If you want the total width to remain within 300px even with padding and borders, you can use box-sizing: border-box; in your CSS.

Hope this clarifies your question! Feel free to ask if you have more queries.
